summary: Half-hour deep dive into repeated CUDA watchdog resets seen on CharonTech's on-prem racks. Root cause unclear: pattern points at short-lived memory spike during KV cache recovery combined with aggressive prefetcher + tiny retry window. We agreed to run an isolated repro with prefetch off, collect nvml/dmesg, and try a conservative retry/backoff patch from Redwood before next call.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-01-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Olivia Hart (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Janelle Park (Redwood Support), Priya Nair (CharonTech Platform), Gonzalo Ruiz (CharonTech SRE), Liam O'Connor (CharonTech CTO), Marta Kovac (CharonTech Infra)

--- Optional auto sections ---
Summary (auto): Repeated device resets, eviction storms during high-concurrency bursts. Possible interplay between prefetcher, KV cache rebuild, and watchdog timing.
Questions (auto): Is eviction synchronous? Are device-resets coming from driver or kernel OOM?

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Olivia: okay good morning everyone, thanks for joining, um let's do quick intros and then Marcus will jump into the traces you shared, um Priya can you confirm the most recent incident timestamp?
[00:08] Priya: yeah, hi all, the spike was on 01/26 at ~02:14 local, we saw a sequence of 3 device resets across two boxes in quick succession, all running the same onprem stack and our patched runtime, uh logs attached on the drive.
[00:18] Marcus: got it, i pulled the nvml dump you uploaded, there's a recurring cuda watchdog event followed by a device reset, but interestingly the memory footprint doesn't look huge - looks like a sudden short-lived allocation then immediate eviction.
[00:29] Gonzalo: yeah that's the weird part - our monitoring shows ephemeral surges, like 100-200ms spikes to high util then boom, watchdog. we initially thought soft oom but the kernel doesn't show the oom-killer, it's a device reset.
[00:40] Janelle: quick note, transcription may mangle some product names, so when you say K V cache i may have spelled it K-V cache or kvcaache in places.
[00:46] Marcus: haha yeah fair. so first hypothesis: rehydration of the KV cache triggers a concurrent prefetching path which allocates a large temporary buffer on the GPU, combined with continuous batching we exceed a short window and the driver watchdog kicks in.
[01:02] Liam: when you say prefetch are you referring to our runtime prefetcher or the model's kv prefetch? we have both enabled.
[01:09] Marcus: both, exactly. there's a runtime-level prefetcher in front of the model-level kv warmup; if both try to populate caches simultaneously we can get contention spikes.
[01:16] Priya: ohhh that makes sense. we did recently bump concurrency to 12 per-GPU for latency reasons.
[01:22] Gonzalo: and we also have aggressive retry set to 0s - we immediately retry a failed token generation which might cause repeated attempts while the device is in a fragile state.
[01:30] Olivia: so then we have three moving parts: prefetcher, kv rehydration, and retry/backoff semantics. any ideas on which to isolate first?
[01:37] Marcus: i recommend disabling runtime prefetch first (flag --no-prefetch) to see if spikes disappear; it's low effort. then reproduce with pinned model version and capture nvml, dmesg, and driver logs.
[01:46] Priya: sure we can try that. question: would changing batching help? we rely on small batches for latency.
[01:52] Marcus: yes there's a tradeoff - smaller batch reduces peak memory at any single op but increases relative overhead; if prefetch is the culprit, batching won't help. if eviction is KV-cache reorg, then spreading work across time helps.
[02:03] Gonzalo: we also observed TCP timeouts on a node around the same window - could networking be exacerbating watchdog triggers?
[02:09] Marcus: possible; if the client stalls waiting for data and the runtime spins, CPU-side stalls can cascade to GPU stalls. we should capture perf traces on the host as well.
[02:17] Liam: ok can you explain the retry window you mentioned? we currently have a 300ms retry window with immediate retry.
[02:23] Marcus: yes so Redwood's runtime will, by default, issue an immediate retry for transient failures up to a short window; unfortunately immediate retries can cause tight retry loops in face of device instability. switching to exponential backoff (50ms -> 200ms -> 800ms) reduces pressure.
[02:35] Priya: are there any risks to backoff for p99 latency? we'll see higher tail for failed requests.
[02:40] Olivia: tradeoff - slightly higher p99 for isolated failures vs systemic outages if devices reset. most enterprise customers prefer stability; we can make backoff configurable per-route.
[02:49] Gonzalo: can Redwood push a canary runtime with a conservative backoff and no prefetch? we'd run it on two nodes.
[02:54] Marcus: yes we can produce a small patch, but we want logs to validate the fix. also i want to call out a pattern seen in the traces: when the kv cache rebuild starts there are rapid small allocations then one larger allocation, the latter correlates with the watchdog. possibly an internal temp buffer for attention caching.
[03:10] Marta: are you talking about the K/V cache fragmentation? we've seen the memory graph show many small free holes.
[03:15] Marcus: exactly, fragmentation + a suddenly-required contiguous buffer -> alloc failure or driver stall leading to watchdog. quantization can exacerbate this if we use BF16 vs int8 code paths due to different kernel memory layouts.
[03:26] Priya: we are using an 8-bit quant profile for cost reasons. could quantization change allocation pattern so drastically?
[03:31] Marcus: yes, int8 kernels sometimes allocate different scratch memory. we should repro with both quant profiles.
[03:38] Olivia: ok list of experiments: 1) run without runtime prefetch, 2) run with exponential backoff, 3) try same workload with fp16 vs int8 kernels, 4) collect host perf (perf, strace) and GPU nvml/dmesg.
[03:52] Priya: noted. how do we collect a kv-cache dump?
[03:56] Marcus: there is a runtime flag to dump kv cache to disk on eviction; i'll send the exact command, it's in the runbook. it will be heavy but helpful.
[04:02] Gonzalo: in your logs you mentioned 'evicton' spelled oddly, is that a mis-parse? what exactly happens during eviction?
[04:07] Marcus: lol yeah auto transcript. eviction is synchronous in our current build - when memory crosses threshold we evict oldest prefixes which triggers writes and rehydration on read; synchronous eviction under load can cause the exact burst we see. we have an async eviction branch that staggers writes but it's still experimental.
[04:20] Liam: can we toggle eviction strategy without rebuilding? maybe config flag?
[04:24] Marcus: short answer: not in the stable runtime; it's a compile-time knob in our older forks. we can run a canary with async eviction for you.
[04:30] Priya: ok great. Marta: network timeouts you mentioned, how to rule them out?
[04:33] Marcus: capture tcpdump around the incident window, check for retransmits; also capture latencies for your backend datastore if the kv is backed by remote store during cold starts. if datastore stalls, pipeline stalls and GPU timetable shifts.
[04:45] Janelle: small note - speaker labels might switch to Speaker 2 or generic names intermittently in the rest of the transcript.
[04:52] Gonzalo: are there any kernel versions incompatible with our driver? we're on 5.15 and driver 525.x.
[04:57] Marcus: driver 525 is okay but there are known intermittent watchog regressions in some 525 builds on certain cards. please capture 'nvidia-smi --query' output and driver release notes; we'll cross-check in our bug tracker.
[05:07] Priya: we can do that. Marcus, you mentioned a small patch to tweak retry semantics - is that low risk?
[05:12] Marcus: it's basically a config change and a tiny backoff wrapper; low risk. we'll also expose it as a per-route config so you can A/B test.
[05:20] Olivia: i'll also share the Redwood checklist for device-reset triage: what to collect, how to tag artifacts, and example nvml/dmesg snippets.
[05:26] Priya: perfect. any concerns with on-prem VPC routing? we run a private control plane over an overlay network, sometimes ARP flaps occur.
[05:34] Marcus: ARP flaps can cause transient stalls in control plane operations which might hold locks; if eviction routines wait on control-plane persistence, that could block. capture system logs too.
[05:44] Gonzalo: curious - do you have a telemetry flag to trace the internal kv->evict->rehydrate path with timestamps so we can see exact timings?
[05:51] Marcus: yes there is a debug mode that timestamps each step. it has some overhead but for a short repro it's fine. i'll send exact flags.
[06:00] Liam: okay let's align on deliverables and owners now.
[06:04] Olivia: action items: Priya captures dumps and nvml by 02/02; Marcus provides repro harness and flags by 02/03; Olivia shares device-reset triage doc and pricing pilot template by 02/04.
[06:14] Priya: confirmed. also can you share any internal incidents similar to this so we can compare?
[06:19] Marcus: yes i'll redact customer names and send two prior incidents where fragmentation + prefetching caused watchdogs.
[06:25] Priya: thanks. final question - is there an immediate mitigation we should apply to reduce customer impact?
[06:30] Olivia: short-term apply conservative backoff and lower per-GPU concurrency by 25% on one pool, route critical traffic to a fallback smaller model if possible.
[06:40] Gonzalo: we'll try that after lunch and report results.
[06:44] Olivia: great, we'll reconvene next week. thanks everyone.
[06:48] (call ends)
